findings.title: v13/v14 get 'a person's first issue due' questions wrong whenever the wording has none of the 15 listed words (they lose to v11/v12; 'which of two' questions are safe)
findings.evidence:
The rule at line 407, `not self.orders or ordered or p.aggregate not in ("earliest","latest")`, keeps a plan that picks by date only when `asks_order` (line 339) finds a word from ORDER_WORDS (line 51). For a person_first question the remaining list, count and single plans always pass this rule, so it is never skipped and the earliest-due plan is dropped.

I asked v11 and v13 (scratchpad/ordlens_corr/probe.py, cases1.json, cases2.json) on the real banks of mdtick, mdplan and mdrep, using reworded person_first questions with the expected answers taken from the sets. 41 of 42 wordings with no order word went from 1.0 in v11 to 0.0 in v13 (the 42nd was already 0 in v11). Examples:
- 'Which of Daniel Cho's tickets has the tightest deadline? Key please.' v11: ENG-42702 (earliest), right. v13: 'ENG-24111, ENG-42702, ENG-991111, ENG-99123' (list).
- 'Which ticket assigned to Daniel Cho is most overdue?' v13: '4' (count).
- 'Which of Priya Desai's tickets is most pressing by due date?' v13: PM-28415 (via assignee_of -> parent_issue -> label -> single).
- 'Which of Daniel Cho's tickets has the closer deadline?' v13: ACMEAI-019447 (via customer_attendees_of).
Other wordings that failed the same way: 'oldest due date', 'minimum due date', 'most time-sensitive', 'What should P work on 1st?', 'due early', 'upcoming', 'needs doing ASAP', 'top of the queue by due date'.

The list is not a closed class. It has 'sooner', 'earlier' and 'later' but not 'closer' or 'nearer' (stems 'clos' and 'near'). It has 'earliest' but not 'early', and it lacks 'oldest', 'upcoming', 'prior', 'overdue', 'pressing' and 'tight'.

v14 behaves the same. With a form of {kind: key, fields: [due_date]}, v11 still gives ENG-42702 but v13 gives the list. Rule 5 runs before the form's field rule (rule 6), so the form's date field cannot bring the plan back.

compare_two is not affected. The 'list of both' plan is already removed by the clue rule (plans.py line 317), so no plan passes rule 5 and it is skipped. I checked 8 wordings for each of 6 pairs, plus cases where the asked kind is None or 'other': all still answer by earliest.

The claims that hold: every person_first and compare_two question in all seen sets (including the _w1, _w2 and _w3 writer sets) uses a listed word. v11 and v12 answers in dev_v11.json and dev_v12.json match the stored pre-commit factbank_v11.jsonl and factbank_v12.jsonl exactly. The tests pass (24).
findings.fix: Widen asks_order before freezing. Possible ways: add the missing comparatives and superlatives ('closer', 'nearer', 'early', 'oldest', 'upcoming', 'prior', 'overdue', 'pressing', 'tightest'); make the rule depend on there being an alternative to the date pick (for example, keep earliest/latest when the question names a single person and asks for one key, i.e. singular 'which ... ticket' or 'which one'); or let the form's date field (v14) override rule 5. Then rerun development. If the list stays as it is, remove the 'closed class' and 'never removes the right plan' claims from the pre-registration (lines 31 and 52).

verdict.reason: I could not refute it; I reproduced it. ORDER_WORDS stems to {after, before, closest, earli, earliest, final, first, last, later, latest, nearest, next, soon, soonest, urgent}. 'closer' (clos), 'nearer' (near), 'early', 'oldest', 'overdue', 'upcoming', 'prior', 'pressing', 'tightest', '1st' and 'ASAP' all give asks_order False. When I ran the reviewer's probe on the real mdtick bank, v11 answers ENG-42702 (Daniel Cho → assignee_of [ticket] → due_date → earliest, which is right) for wordings such as 'tightest deadline', 'most overdue', 'oldest due date', 'due early', 'closer deadline', 'upcoming', 'ASAP', 'top of the queue by due date' and 'due 1st'. v13 drops the earliest plan in check rule 5 and answers with the label list, the count '4', or a wrong single key reached over an unrelated path (customer_attendees_of → crm_account_id). Rule 5 is not skipped because the list, count and single plans pass it. v14 cannot recover this through the form. Rule 5 runs before rule 6, and field_fits returns True for a key-kind list plan, so the form's due_date field does not bring the date plan back. A plain-quoted "first" is also lost, because quoted text is ignored. compare_two is safe, as the finding says: the clue rule has already removed the alternatives. The pre-registration calls the 15 words "a closed class", and that is false: it keeps 'closest' and 'nearest' but not 'closer' and 'nearer', and 'earliest'/'earlier' but not 'early'. The list was also built from the earlier writers' wordings, which already varied a lot (nearest, urgent, before all the others, lands soonest, ship first). For the test itself: each person_first wording template covers about half of a set's 6–8 person_first questions, roughly 3–4 of the ~40 non-action questions. If one sealed writer's person_first wording uses a word outside the list, v11 → v13 drops by about 0.075–0.1 on 'other questions', which fails rule 2 (≥ −0.03). Widening the list before freezing would change that number and possibly the verdict. Fixing it before freezing does not break the blind protocol, because the wordings are unseen.

findings.title: No decision rule covers the ordering questions; one wrong person_first answer per test set passes rule 2
findings.evidence:
The pre-registration (line 117) says the ordering questions are where 'the check must do no harm'. But order_test only reports m["ordering_questions"]. The only rule that could catch harm there is rule 2, which pools them with all other questions: `at_least(d(other_questions v13, v11), -0.03)`.

The earlier sets have 40 to 42 other questions each (mdtick 40, mdplan 42, mdrep 41), of which 6 to 8 are person_first. One person_first question lost to the failure above costs 1/40 = -0.025, which passes -0.03. So v13 can get 1 in 6 to 8 'first issue due' questions newly wrong (12 to 17% of that group) and every rule still reads as met.
findings.fix: Before freezing, add a rule on m['ordering_questions']: v13 >= v11 and v14 >= v12 (or at most 0.0x below), or no ordering question newly wrong. Also report the questions that changed, one by one.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and could not. Every claim checks out.

1. **No rule covers the ordering questions.** In order_test (cie/src/cie/eval/factbank_multi.py), m["ordering_questions"] is computed and reported, but none of rules 1 to 7 reads it. The pre-registration (lines 116-117) calls this group the place where "the check must do no harm". Its only protection is rule 2: `at_least(d(other_questions v13, v11), -0.03)`, taken over all non-action questions together.

2. **The counts are right.** The earlier sets have 40 to 42 non-action questions each (mdtick 40, mdplan 42, mdrep 41) and 6 to 8 person_first questions. Losing one question entirely costs 1/40 = 0.025, or 0.024 on 41 or 42. That passes the -0.03 threshold.
   - Rules 1 and 3 look only at action items.
   - Rule 4 looks only at earlier sets, which are unaffected.
   - Rules 5 and 7 have wide margins.
   - Rule 6 compares the test set with its changed copy, which uses the same wordings, so both lose together.
   - So one such loss passes every rule.

3. **The failure can actually happen.** I ran mdtick with the v11 and v13 lessons on reworded questions that contain no word from ORDER_WORDS. Words like "closer", "nearer", "more overdue", "urgently", "most pressing" and "top of the queue" are all missed by asks_order.
   - **compare_two is immune.** Check 3 leaves only the earliest plan for two named items, so check 5 is skipped. v11 and v13 both scored 1.0 on all four reworded probes.
   - **person_first breaks.** "which one is most pressing by due date?" and "What's at the top of Priya Desai's queue by due date?" score 1.0 under v11. Under v13 the plan changes from assignee_of → due_date → earliest to assignee_of → label → list. v13 answers with all four keys and scores 0.0, because person_first is SINGLE_KEY and needs an exact match.

**What softens it:**
- None of the roughly 170 ordering questions in the 10 earlier sets lacks an order word, so the trigger is unlikely.
- Any harm would still appear in the reported ordering_questions numbers.
- The -0.03 pooled no-harm rule is copied from the ticket test.

Still, v13 differs from v11 only through this one deterministic check, and its only way to do harm falls in the person_first group. The rules let one such loss in about 7 there go through with every rule met, even though the text promises no harm there.

The probe script is at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-integratedai/275b943f-979b-5741-9af5-2a07879accea/scratchpad/refute_ordrule/probe.py.

findings.title: 'Outside quoted titles' is really 'outside any straight-quoted text': a quoted order word is dropped, while curly-quoted titles are still read
findings.evidence:
question_words (line 592) removes every span matching re.sub(r'"[^"]*"', ...), whether or not it is a title, and leaves curly quotes untouched. I checked the results:
- 'Of all the tickets assigned to Daniel Cho, which one is due "first"? Key please.' gives asks_order=False. On mdtick, v11 answers ENG-42702 (1.0) and v13 answers 'ENG-24111, ENG-42702, ENG-991111, ENG-99123' (0.0). It is the same with a key/due_date form.
- The same question with curly quotes around first gives asks_order=True and is answered right.
- 'Who took “Next steps for pilot”? List their tickets.' gives asks_order=True, so a curly-quoted action-item or meeting title that contains an order word ('Next steps…', 'Final…', or the 'Urgent: Fallback policy & long-tail error mitigation sync' meeting in mdblind) turns the check off, and v13 then gives v11's wrong answer.
- Single-quoted titles ('Final review') are also read.
No earlier set used curly quotes (I checked every questions.jsonl). The test's new writers, including 'a VP on a phone', may.
findings.fix: Strip only what titled() resolves to a real title, or strip curly and single quotes the same way and keep an order word when the quoted span is just that word (one or two words that are all in ORDER_WORDS). At least correct the pre-registration's 'outside quoted titles' description.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed how the code behaves. question_words (plans.py:590-592) blanks every span inside straight double quotes and leaves curly and single quotes alone, and Planner.asks_order uses it. Results: due "first" (straight quotes) gives False. The same with curly quotes gives True. A curly-quoted "Next steps for pilot" gives True, and 'Final review' in single quotes gives True. So the pre-registration's "outside quoted titles" really means "outside any straight double-quoted text". That is a small gap between the wording and the code, and a robustness edge case.

It does not matter for this test, for four reasons:
(1) Title quoting comes from the writers' templates ("{t}", "{m}"). In all 12 earlier blind writers (writers.json and wordings.json for factbank_general, llm, plan and ticket), every {t} and {m} is in straight double quotes (6/6 in each file). None of those 120 wordings puts quotes around anything else, so none quotes an order word. No questions.jsonl in mdtrain through mdtick has a curly quote.
(2) Treating only straight quotes as title quotes is the whole system's frozen rule: v9's titled(), plain_words and question_words all work that way, and nothing normalises curly quotes. A writer using curly quotes would break title recognition for v11 and v12 in exactly the same way. That is not a v13-specific unfairness.
(3) The curly-title case can only make v13 match v11 (the check does nothing). It does no harm, and it needs an order word inside a title: only 1 of 78 earlier action-item questions has one (mdblind's "Urgent: ..."). So the expected effect on rule 1 is about zero.
(4) The harm case needs a writer to put quotes around the order word itself (due "first"). That never happened in 120 earlier wordings.

At most, the pre-registration could say "outside straight double-quoted text (titles)". No test number or verdict plausibly depends on this.

findings.title: Words of order used in passing turn the fix off, including 'soon' (from stemming 'sooner'), 'lasting', and 'not just the first one'
findings.evidence:
stem('sooner') is 'soon', so bare 'soon' counts as an order word, as does 'as soon as you can'. Also stem('lasting') = stem('lasted') = 'last' and stem('finals') = 'final'. Any order word anywhere in the question counts, even when negated.

On mdtick action_owner_issues-027, -036 and -041, the plain wording is v11 0.4 and v13 1.0. Adding 'Need them as soon as you can.', 'Need them before my 1:1.', 'I'll follow up after standup.', 'Thanks, last thing for today.' or 'All of them, not just the first one.' brings v13 back to 0.4 (only the first-due key), the same as v11 (cases3.json). The last case asks outright for all of them and still gets only the first.

In development, mdwords' action items start with 'After "…"' and mdtick's person_count and pr_issue questions say 'before interviews', so this wording is common.

It is not a regression against v11, but it limits rule 1 (+0.15 on action items), and the pre-registered list names 'sooner', not 'soon'.
findings.fix: Write the actual stems into the pre-registration (soon, earli, ...). Consider matching order words only near the thing asked for (for example 'due/deadline ... first/soonest', or 'which ... first') rather than anywhere in the question, and ignore negated uses ('not just the first').

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and couldn't. Every concrete claim checks out.

**What the code does** (cie/src/cie/factbank/plans.py):
- `ORDER_WORDS` is built with engine.stem. The set it actually holds is {after, before, closest, earli, earliest, final, first, last, later, latest, nearest, next, soon, soonest, urgent}.
- `stem('sooner')` is 'soon', so a bare "soon" counts as an order word. So do 'lasting' and 'lasted' (both stem to 'last') and 'finals' (stems to 'final').
- `asks_order` checks whether any word of the question, outside quoted titles, is in that set. It does not look at context or negation.
- So `Planner.asks_order` returns True for each of: "Need them as soon as you can.", "All of them, not just the first one.", "Thanks, last thing for today.", "I'll follow up after standup."

**My own probe** (scratchpad/refute_soon/p.py; it does not use the reviewer's cases3.json):
- I ran all 10 action_owner_issues questions in mdtick with the real v11 and v13 lessons (orders False and True).
- 8 of them are fixed by v13 on the plain wording, e.g. 027, 036 and 041 go from v11 0.4 (earliest) to v13 1.0 (list).
- Adding any of the six suffixes puts v13 back on the 'earliest' plan with exactly v11's score, on all 8. The suffixes are "as soon as you can", "Need them soon", "before my 1:1", "after standup", "last thing for today" and "All of them, not just the first one".
- So the last suffix asks outright for all of them and still gets only the first due.
- Suffixes without an order word keep v13's gain: "All of them please" and "Need them ASAP" both stay at 1.0 (list).

**Development sets:**
- mdwords: 5 of 8 action items contain 'after'.
- No other development set has an action item with an order word.
- Bare 'soon' comes into the set only through training's "which is due sooner", so the collision follows from stemming.

**Why it is low and doesn't decide the test:**
- It is never worse than v11: rule 5 only ever removes plans.
- The pre-registration already says the words are "(stemmed)" and that uses in passing make the check "simply do nothing".
- The code is frozen by commit, so the behaviour can be reproduced exactly.
- The limitation can only shrink the measured gain on rule 1 (v13 − v11 on action items). Whether it does depends on whether the sealed wordings put such words in action items, which can't be known without opening blind5. The test stays fair; it would simply measure this limitation.
- A clarifying line in the pre-registration would help: the effective stems include 'soon' and 'earli', and negated uses also count.

findings.title: Ordinal numbers ('1st') are never read as words of order because question_words keeps letters only
findings.evidence: question_words tokenizes with re.findall(r"[a-z]+", ...), so '1st' becomes 'st' (and likewise '2nd' becomes 'nd'). Planner.asks_order('Which is due 1st?') is False. On mdtick, 'Which of Daniel Cho's tickets is due 1st? Key please.': v11 1.0 (ENG-42702), v13 0.0 (list of 4 keys), and the same with a key/due_date form. 'What should Ravi Desai work on 1st?' on mdplan: v11 1.0, v13 0.0.
findings.fix: Tokenize with [a-z0-9]+ in asks_order, or map '1st' to 'first' before matching (leave question_words alone for the frozen AskedKind).

verdict.reason:
The defect is real. question_words (cie/src/cie/factbank/plans.py, line 590) splits words with re.findall(r"[a-z]+", ...), and Planner.asks_order matches those words against ORDER_WORDS. So "1st" becomes "st" and "2nd" becomes "nd", and neither counts as a word of order. I ran it directly: asks_order('Which is due 1st?') returns False, and question_words gives {'which','due','st','is'}.

On the mdtick bank with the mdtrain plan_lessons_v11 and v13 files, no form:
- "Which of Daniel Cho's tickets is due 1st? Key please.": v11 answers ENG-42702 (Daniel Cho → assignee_of [ticket] → due_date → earliest). v13 answers ENG-24111, ENG-42702, ENG-991111, ENG-99123 (→ label → list). The same question with "first" gives ENG-42702 under both.
- The set's own person_first wording with "soonest" replaced by "1st" fails the same way under v13.
- On mdplan, "of Ravi Desai's Linear tickets, which one's due 1st? gimme the key" gives ENG-997888 under v11 and a list of 3 keys under v13.

One of the reviewer's examples is wrong. "What should Ravi Desai work on 1st?" gets "medium" (customer_impact) from v11 as well, so v11 does not score 1.0 there and it shows no v11-to-v13 drop. The mdtick example reproduces exactly.

Frozen versions are not affected: with orders=False, check 5 always passes.

Why it probably doesn't matter for the test: none of the ~650 questions in the earlier sets uses a written-out number like "1st", "2nd" or "3rd". That covers mdtrain, mdtrainv9, mdtest, mdfresh, mdwords, mdblind, mdllm, mdplan, mdrep and mdtick, about 180 of them asking for an order (person_first or compare_two), and the wordings in factbank_multi.py don't use one either. The pre-registration defines the check as an explicit list of words. If a sealed wording does say "1st", the frozen v13 would rightly be scored as failing it, and the report already counts the ordering questions with no word of order. So fairness holds.

The risk is not zero. Each kind has two wordings, so one person_first wording with "1st" could cost about 3 of the roughly 40 non-action-item questions, a drop of about 0.075. That is enough to fail rule 2, which allows −0.03. The "VP on a phone" writer is the likeliest to write that way. Matching [a-z0-9]+ inside asks_order would close this before freezing and would not change any development result. I can't confirm the sealed wordings use numbers like this, and the base rate is zero, so I don't count it as changing a test number.

findings.title: Rule 3's 'not measurable' check uses v12's score, but the pre-registration ties it to v11's
findings.evidence: The pre-registration's 'What decides' section says: 'If v11 already scores 0.9 or more on the action items ... Rules 1 and 3 are then reported as not measurable.' order_test does this for rule 1 with `... if ai["v11"] is not None and ai["v11"] < ROOM else None`, but rule 3 uses `... if ai["v12"] is not None and ai["v12"] < ROOM else None`. On the test set v11 and v12 can land on different sides of 0.9 on the action items, because the form changes answers: on mdwords and mdblind, for example, v12 differs from v11. If v11 >= 0.9 > v12, rule 3 is judged when the pre-registration says it should read 'not measurable'. If v12 >= 0.9 > v11, rule 3 reads 'not measurable' when it should be judged. The ticket test, the precedent, used one shared condition for rules 1 and 3. The docstring ('when the version before already scores ROOM') matches the code, not the pre-registration.
findings.fix: Use v11's score for both rules: `measurable = ai["v11"] is not None and ai["v11"] < ROOM`, then apply it to rules 1 and 3. If v12 is the intended condition for rule 3, change the pre-registration before freezing it instead.

verdict.reason:
The mismatch is real. In cie/docs/FACTBANK_ORDER_PREREGISTRATION.md, lines 135-136 say: "If v11 already scores 0.9 or more on the action items ... Rules 1 and 3 are then reported as not measurable." So one condition, v11's action-item score, is meant to govern both rules. The code in cie/src/cie/eval/factbank_multi.py:876 bases rule 1 on v11 (`ai["v11"] < ROOM`), but line 880 bases rule 3 on v12 (`ai["v12"] < ROOM`). The precedent agrees with the finding: ticket_test (lines 804-812) uses one shared `measurable` flag for rules 1 and 3. No test in tests/test_factbank_multi.py covers order_test's ROOM logic, so nothing catches the difference.

Part of the reviewer's evidence is wrong. I compared every set in the development results (dev_v11.json, dev_v12.json, 19 sets). On the action-item questions, v11 and v12 score exactly the same in all of them, for example mdtick 0.600/0.600, mdblind 0.963/0.963 and mdwords 1.0/1.0. The v11-vs-v12 differences on mdwords, mdblind and other sets are all on pr_issue and ticket_link questions, never action items.

So the two conditions give different answers only if v11 and v12 land on opposite sides of 0.9 on the test's action items. Development never showed that, and the test is built to trigger the mistake (v11 scored 0.6 on the ticket test). Rule 3 also does not decide the outcome: the pre-registration says rules 1 and 2 decide.

Even so, the frozen code would implement a different rule-3 condition from the frozen document. Since neither can change after freezing, this should be reconciled first: either use v11 for both rules, or rewrite the pre-registration to say v12 for rule 3.

findings.title: single_writers.py builds a writer's folder from that writer's raw wordings, including the one the selection rule rejected; this time one was rejected
findings.evidence: The script is the ticket test's, with only the paths changed. For writer i it uses `w = {key: [x["wording"]] for x in writer{i}.json}` and calls `fm.questions(...)`, which runs `w.format(**fmt)` on every wording. The ticket and planner tests both printed that no wording was replaced, so this path never met an invalid wording. This pre-registration says 'one wording was replaced', so mdord_w1 or mdord_w2 will contain a wording the rule judged invalid. Earlier tests define invalid as not using each placeholder exactly once, or longer than 200 characters (FACTBANK_GENERAL_PREREGISTRATION.md). What happens depends on the kind of fault. (a) An unknown placeholder or a stray brace makes .format raise KeyError or ValueError. Under `set -e`, run_order.sh then stops after the set is drawn and before any arm answers, and the traceback may show part of a sealed wording. (b) A missing placeholder passes the script's id/expected/pieces assertion silently and leaves a question that does not name its subject, which lowers that writer's per-writer numbers. (c) A doubled placeholder is harmless. I could not check which case applies without opening blind5.
findings.fix: In single_writers.py, check each writer's wordings with the selection rule's validity test. For an invalid wording, either use the stand-in from wordings.json (writer 3's wording) or leave that key out of the writer's folder. Print only the number of wordings affected, so the protocol stays blind. Fix this before the run, not after a crash.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute the mechanism. I did not open blind5. One attempt to pull the selection script out of the session transcript was blocked by the permission system, and I did not try again.

1) What the code does: cie/docs/benchmarks/factbank_order/single_writers.py is the same file as scratchpad/ord/single_writers.py. It differs from tick/single_writers.py and plan9/single_writers.py only in its paths. For each writer it builds `w = {key: [x["wording"]]}` straight from writer{i}.json, with no validity check. Then fm.questions() runs `w.format(**fmt)` on every wording (factbank_multi.py:292-296). The only check that follows compares id, expected and pieces. It never looks at the question text.

2) The pre-registration says a wording was replaced: FACTBANK_ORDER_PREREGISTRATION.md lines 96-97 say "A script applied it and printed only that one wording was replaced". Under the selection rule, writer 3 only stands in for an invalid wording from writer 1 or 2. So mdord_w1 or mdord_w2 will be built from a wording the rule rejected. The ticket and planner tests replaced none, so this path has never run on a rejected wording.

3) I reproduced each case on the ticket set: mdtick, seed 44, writer 1 of tick/blind4, which is not sealed, with one wording swapped for a synthetic one.
- Missing placeholder: the check passes, and the question reads "who owns the linked ticket?", with no subject.
- Doubled placeholder: the check passes and the question is fine.
- Over 200 characters: the check passes.
- Unknown placeholder: KeyError('num').
- Stray brace: ValueError("Single '}' encountered").
- Key absent from the writer's file: KeyError.
Under `set -e`, either error stops the frozen run_order.sh at single_writers.py, before the arms are asked.

4) What it touches: order_test uses the writer folders only for m["writers"], which is reported. None of rules 1-7 uses them, so a verdict can change only if the run stops. Which case applies depends on the sealed wording, so whether it actually bites is unconfirmed. It could be harmless (doubled or long), it could lower one writer's reported numbers (missing placeholder), or it could stop the frozen run and force a change to the script after the freeze (unknown placeholder, stray brace or missing key). The suggested fix is cheap to apply before the freeze: apply the rule's validity check and use writer 3's stand-in, or leave the key out, printing only a count.

Side check: a list of one wording and the set's pair of wordings use up the random generator's numbers in the same way, so the id check itself will not fail.

findings.title: Between 0.85 and 0.9, rule 1 is judged but cannot be met
findings.evidence: ROOM = 0.9, and rule 1 requires v13 - v11 >= +0.15. Because v13 <= 1.0, any v11 score on the action items in [0.85, 0.9) leaves a maximum gain below 0.15 (for example, 1.0 - 0.875 = 0.125). Rule 1 is then reported 'not met', not 'not measurable', even if v13 answers every action item correctly. The pre-registration says rules 1 and 2 decide whether the check works. The test set is likely to have 8 to 10 action items (the eight earlier sets have 8, 9, 8, 9, 8, 8, 9 and 10), so v11 = 7/8 = 0.875 (one item wrong, the rest right) is a plausible score. Rule 3 has the same gap with v12. The code follows the pre-registration here; the gap is in the design.
findings.fix: Before freezing, set ROOM to 1 - 0.15 = 0.85, so rule 1 is judged only when a +0.15 gain is possible, or state in the pre-registration how a score in [0.85, 0.9) is to be read.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and could not. In cie/src/cie/eval/factbank_multi.py, order_test judges rule 1 whenever ai["v11"] < ROOM (0.9) and requires at_least(round(v13 - v11, 3), 0.15). Rule 3 does the same with v12 and v14. Action items (kind action_owner_issues) are scored by F1. They are not in SINGLE_KEY, so partial scores are possible, and share() rounds the mean to 3 decimals.

I ran the code's own at_least and ROOM. With v13 = 1.0 and v11 at 0.875, 0.889 or 0.883, the gap is 0.125, 0.111 or 0.117. Each of those v11 scores is under ROOM, so the rule is judged, and each returns False. to_markdown then prints 'not met', not 'not measurable'. At v11 = 0.85 exactly the rule is met (0.15 >= 0.15), so the gap is (0.85, 0.9).

These scores are reachable on the likely test set:
- **8 items:** two first-ticket-only misses at F1 0.5 give 0.875; misses at 0.667 and 0.5 give 0.896.
- **9 items:** two misses at 0.5, or three at 0.667, give 0.889.
- **10 items:** misses at 0.667, 0.5 and 0.667 give 0.883.

The earlier sets have 8, 9, 9, 8, 9, 8, 8, 9 and 10 action items (dev_v11.json). On them v11 scores 0.938, 1.0, 0.963, 0.6 and so on on the action items. Every v11 miss there was the first-due kind that v13 fixes, so v13 = 1.0 everywhere. Results per writer differ: on the ticket test, v11 scores 0.6 / 0.6 / 1.0 on writers 1 / 2 / 3. So a mixed result with 2 or 3 misses is plausible.

The pre-registration's own reason for 'not measurable' is 'there is no room for it to help'. In this band the rule cannot be met even if v13 is perfect, yet it is still reported 'not met'. Rules 1 and 2 'decide whether the check works', so that would read as a failed check. The test set has not been drawn yet: run_order.sh builds mdord only after the pre-registration commit. The gap can therefore still be fixed before freezing, either with ROOM = 0.85 or with a stated reading for this band. The code matches the pre-registration, so this is a flaw in the design, not a bug in the code. It is low-probability, but it would change the verdict on rules 1 and 3 in a plausible range of outcomes.

findings.title: Rule 1 (and rule 3) is evaluated, and can only come out 'not met', whenever v11 lands between 0.85 and 0.9 on the action items
findings.evidence: Line 831 sets ROOM = 0.9. Lines 875-880 then apply at_least(v13 - v11, 0.15) whenever ai['v11'] < ROOM (rule 3 does the same with v12/v14). The best v13 can score is 1.0, so for any v11 above 0.85 the gain is below 0.15 and the rule is reported 'not met' even when v13 fixes every first-due answer. Realistic cases: (a) 10 action items, two 4-ticket owners answered with only the first due (F1 0.4 each): v11 = 0.88, best possible gain 0.12. (b) 9 items failing at 0.5 and 0.4: v11 = 0.878. Every action-item owner has 2-4 Linear issues (units(): 2 <= len(by_person[o]) <= 4), so one fixed question is worth 0.333, 0.5 or 0.6 divided by n (8-10). That is +0.033 to +0.075 per question, so the +0.15 bar means 2 to 5 fixed questions depending on how many tickets the owners hold. The room is also measured as 1 - v11, which counts failures v13 cannot fix (another owner, Jira vs Linear, not found). In the ticket test, v9 scored 0.0 on 3 of 10 action items for reasons outside the order check. Per the pre-registration, rules 1 and 2 decide whether the check works, so this gap can by itself produce a 'failed' verdict.
findings.fix: Before freezing, set ROOM to at most 1 - 0.15 = 0.85. Better: tie measurability and the bar to the room the check could actually recover. Count it from v11's own stored answers on the test set: action items whose chosen plan aggregates earliest/latest and whose question has no word of order (both visible in v11's 'reason' and Planner.asks_order). For example, measurable if that recoverable room is >= 0.15, and the rule is met if v13 recovers at least X% of it.

verdict.reason:
Confirmed in the code and the draft pre-registration, which agree with each other. factbank_multi.py:831 sets ROOM = 0.9. Lines 875-880 judge rule 1 as at_least(round(v13 - v11, 3), 0.15) whenever v11 < 0.9, and rule 3 the same way with v14/v12. The draft says the same thing ("If v11 already scores 0.9 or more ... not measurable" and the +0.15 bar). Since v13 can score at most 1.0, any v11 in (0.85, 0.9) makes the rule measurable but impossible to meet.

I ran the real ROOM and at_least on plausible outcomes. A perfect v13 = 1.0 still gives "not met" for:
- 8 items with 2 fails at 0.5 (v11 0.875)
- 9 items with 2 fails at 0.5 (0.889)
- 10 items with 2 fails at 0.4 (0.88)
- 10 items with fails at 0.5 and 0.4 (0.89)
- 9 items with 3 fails at 0.667 (0.889)

The per-fail scores follow from units() at line 238 (each owner has 2-4 tickets), so a first-due-only answer scores 2/(k+1) = 0.667, 0.5 or 0.4.

These cases are realistic. Earlier sets had 8-10 action items. In the dev rows, v11 failed on 0, 1, or 8 action items per set, and the ticket test showed strong wording dependence: writers 1 and 2 had 8 fails each, writer 3 had none. So 2-3 fails on the new writers' wordings is a likely outcome.

Since the draft names rules 1 and 2 as the ones that decide whether the check works, that band could produce a 'not met' / failed verdict no matter how good v13 is. That makes the test unfair, and the design is still a draft. It can be fixed before freezing by setting ROOM to 0.85 or less, or by tying the bar to the room v13 could actually recover.

The secondary point (1 - v11 also counts failures v13 cannot fix) is more a design choice. The core dead-band claim stands on its own.

findings.title: Development says 'not measurable' is the likely outcome of rule 1, and the pre-registration does not say what follows from it
findings.evidence: I recomputed v11's mean on the action items for all 19 development set/wording variants in dev_v11.json. It is >= 0.9 on 17 of them: mdtrain 0.938, mdtest 1.0, mdfresh 1.0, mdwords 1.0, mdblind 0.963, mdllm 1.0, mdplan/_w1/_w2/_w3 0.938, mdrep/_w1/_w2/_w3 1.0, and mdtick_w3 (ticket writer 3) 1.0. Only ticket-test writers 1 and 2 ('which tickets are assigned to them? ... keys') are below 0.9 (0.600). So unless the new writers happen to phrase action items like those two, rules 1 and 3 will read 'not measurable'. Lines 133-136 say rules 1 and 2 decide and that 1 and 3 are then 'reported as not measurable'. They do not say whether v13/v14 is then adopted, rejected, or left unconfirmed. In that case, rules 4 and 7 are already known to pass, rule 5's training half is fixed, and rule 2 is likely. A write-up could then call v13 'passed every measurable rule' when its benefit was never tested on unseen data.
findings.fix: Pre-register the outcome of the not-measurable branch explicitly. For example: 'If rule 1 is not measurable, the test gives no evidence that the check helps; v13 is not adopted on this test's strength, and only the no-harm rules are reported.' Also state the prior from development: 17 of 19 earlier wordings leave no room.

verdict.reason:
Both premises of the finding are weaker than claimed, and the gap it names is already covered by the document's own logic and by the project's usual practice.

1. The development prior is overstated and mostly drawn from a different situation. I recomputed v11 on the action items from dev_v11.json. 16 of 19 variants score 0.9 or more, not 17: the combined mdtick is 0.600 and was left out of the count. More importantly, 15 of those 19 variants name "Linear" in every action-item question, because their briefs said "Linear issue". The order test reuses the ticket brief, which names no tracker (prereg line 94). Only five earlier wordings name no tracker: mdtick_w1 0.600, mdtick_w2 0.600, mdtick_w3 1.0, mdplan_w3 0.938 and mdrep_w3 1.0. The three that pass all say "list"; the two that fail say "which tickets ... keys". In the only earlier test that used this same brief, both of the writers that supply the drawn pair (1 and 2) scored 0.600, which leaves plenty of room for rule 1's +0.15. So development does not show that "not measurable" is the likely outcome. Whether there is room is genuinely uncertain.

2. The not-measurable branch is not left open. Line 134 says "Rules 1 and 2 decide whether the check works." If rule 1 cannot be measured, then by that sentence the check is not shown to work. None of this project's pre-registrations has an adopt-or-reject step; they fix rule verdicts. The ticket pre-registration used the same structure ("reported as not measurable"), and the ticket write-up reported its verdicts plainly. order_test in cie/src/cie/eval/factbank_multi.py (around lines 874-880 and 933) returns None for rules 1 and 3 when the earlier version's score is at or above ROOM, and prints "not measurable". It computes no combined verdict like "passed every measurable rule" that a write-up could lean on. The worry that someone might spin the result is speculative, and it would contradict line 134.

3. Adding the suggested sentence would not change any test number, any rule verdict, or how the arms are compared. At most it is an optional wording clarification. One small difference from the ticket pre-registration: this one drops the explicit "not as met or not met" and the line that per-writer rules are reported "for information". Per-writer results are still listed under "Also reported" (line 142), and the meaning is implied, so this does not affect the test.

findings.title: The claim that every earlier ordering question uses a word of order is true, but only because ORDER_WORDS was built from those wordings; 'urgent' is not a word of time order
findings.evidence: I checked all 86 compare_two/person_first wordings in T (training and held-out), RETEST, NEW_WORDS, BLIND and BLIND2. I also checked docs/benchmarks/factbank_{general,llm,plan,ticket}/writers.json and wordings.json, plan9/blind3/*, tick/blind4/* and chosen_wordings{,2}.json, plus the drawn questions.jsonl of every work folder. Every one asks for an order, so the claim at lines 51-52 of the pre-registration is literally true. But three wordings are covered only by a word that appears in no other ordering wording: NEW_WORDS 'most urgent by date' ('urgent'), RETEST 'the nearest deadline' ('nearest'), and RETEST 'comes due before all the others' ('before'). Without those words, the mdwords and mdfresh person_first questions in those wordings would lose the first-due plan, and 'no question got worse' would not hold. The pre-registration admits the list was fixed after reading the wordings (line 31). It still presents full coverage as evidence that 'the check never removes the right plan', which is circular, and calls the list 'English words of time order, a closed class', which 'urgent' is not. Unseen phrasings such as 'most pressing', 'tightest deadline', 'coming up', 'oldest', 'most recent' or 'ASAP' are not in the list. I verified the development table and the per-question claims from dev_*.json and the stored answers. dev v11/v12 answers equal the stored factbank_v11/v12.jsonl on every set, the committed development.json equals the dev_*.json reps, and my own re-run reproduced mdtick and mdplan. Every change is a gain on an action item and no question got worse. The same holds on the changed copies (mdchanged_fixed, mdfreshchanged_fixed, mdwordschanged_fixed, mdblindchanged_fixed, mdllmchanged, mdplanchanged, mdrepchanged, mdtickchanged) and on mdtrainall.
findings.fix: In the pre-registration, mark the coverage result as true by construction, not as development evidence. Name the words added to cover specific earlier wordings ('urgent', 'nearest', 'before'), and drop the 'closed class of time-order words' wording. Rely on the test's report of ordering questions without a word of order (and on finding 4's rule) as the real check.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and couldn't. Every factual claim in the finding holds.

1. **Three words each cover exactly one wording.** I ran plans.question_words with ORDER_WORDS over every compare_two and person_first wording. That covered T (training and held-out), RETEST, NEW_WORDS, BLIND and BLIND2 in src/cie/eval/factbank_multi.py, plus the writers.json of factbank_general, factbank_llm, factbank_plan and factbank_ticket, and the wordings.json of factbank_plan and factbank_ticket. Every wording hits at least one order word. But 'urgent' (NEW_WORDS 'most urgent by date'), 'nearest' (RETEST 'the nearest deadline') and 'before' (RETEST 'comes due before all the others') each hit exactly one wording. No other wording uses them. 'closest', 'next', 'last', 'latest', 'later', 'final' and 'after' appear in no ordering wording at all.

2. **The no-loss result depends on those three words.** I built a copy of dev.py in memory with plans.ORDER_WORDS minus {urgent, nearest, before} and ran v13 on two sets:
   - mdwords drops from 0.877 to 0.848: person_first-005 and person_first-009 go from 1 to 0.
   - mdfresh drops from 0.984 to 0.889: person_first-002, -004, -006, -008, -010 and -012 go from 1 to 0.
   - In each case the bank falls back to a 'label → list' or parent plan instead of the first due.
   So 'no question anywhere got worse' rests on words added to cover those particular development wordings. Full coverage of the earlier sets was guaranteed by how the list was made, so it is not evidence about new wordings.

3. **The pre-registration overstates the list.** Line 31 says 'These are English words of time order, a closed class'. 'urgent' is a word of priority, not time order, and 'nearest'/'closest' are distance words used about time. Lines 51-52 then present full coverage as the reason 'the check never removes the right plan'. The draft does disclose that the list was fixed after reading the wordings (lines 31-32), and the section is labelled as being on seen sets. That softens the problem but doesn't remove it.

**Why it doesn't matter for the test:** the fix is wording in the pre-registration only. It changes no code, lessons, test number or verdict. The test stays fair:
- ORDER_WORDS is frozen before the sealed wordings are read.
- Rule 2 (per-question no-harm) catches order questions that lose the right plan because their phrasing has no listed word.
- The pre-registration already promises to report how many order questions use no word of order.

Correcting the text before the freeze is cheap, since the frozen document will otherwise carry the inaccurate 'closed class' claim. I modified no repository file. The checks ran from scratch scripts in the scratchpad.

findings.title: Nothing protects the questions that do ask for an order: rule 2's -0.03 allows one of them to be lost outright
findings.evidence: Lines 116-117 say the ordering questions are where 'the check must do no harm', but no rule covers them. order_test only reports m['ordering_questions'] and the count without a word of order. They are judged only inside rule 2: per-question mean over the ~40 non-action questions, v13 >= v11 - 0.03. compare_two and person_first are single-key kinds scored 0/1 (own_score, SINGLE_KEY), so losing one is -1/40 = -0.025 and still passes. Losing exactly the failure this check can cause (an ordering question phrased without a listed word) therefore passes the no-harm rule once per test set.
findings.fix: Add a pre-registered rule on the ordering group, for example v13 >= v11 on compare_two/person_first questions (and the same for v14 vs v12). Or tighten rule 2 so that a single lost question fails.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and couldn't. The finding holds in the code, in the numbers and in a real run.

1. **No rule covers the ordering questions.** Lines 116-117 of the doc say the check "must do no harm" on them. But `order_test` (factbank_multi.py ~L857) only reports `ordering_questions` and the `without_a_word_of_order` count. None of rules 1-7 judges that group. They are judged only inside rule 2: per-question share over the questions that are not action items, `at_least(d(v13, v11), -0.03)`.

2. **One lost question passes rule 2.** Every earlier set has 50 questions, 8-10 of them action items, so about 40-42 others. `compare_two` and `person_first` are scored 0 or 1 (`SINGLE_KEY` in `own_score`). One loss gives d = -0.024 or -0.025, which is ≥ -0.03 and passes. Two losses fail.

3. **The harm actually happens.** I reworded the mdtick ordering questions without a listed word and ran the frozen v11 and v13 lessons (scratchpad/verify_ordrule/probe.py).
   - **`person_first`:** "which ticket is most pressing by due date?" and "which has the tightest deadline?" scored v11 1.0 and v13 0.0 on all 12 tries. Check 5 removes the earliest plan and other plans survive, so the check is not skipped.
   - **`compare_two`:** stayed at 1.0 for both.
   - So a `person_first` wording without a listed word is lost outright.
   - **No offset:** in development v13 never gained on a question that is not an action item, so nothing else in rule 2 makes up for the loss.
   - **No noise excuse:** v13 and v11 share their weights and are deterministic, so any loss is the check's doing.

**What softens it:** a wording is a template. Each writer gives one `person_first` wording, drawn at random for each of the roughly 6-8 `person_first` questions. A missing word therefore usually costs about 3-4 questions (around -0.07), and rule 2 catches that. The gap is narrower than the finding suggests: it is the case where such a template is drawn only once, or one question is otherwise lost. The doc also reports the group and its count.

**Why it still matters before freezing:** the doc states a no-harm requirement on this group and has no rule to back it. In a plausible outcome the verdict "the check works" would be issued while that requirement is broken. Rule 2 also has no v14-vs-v12 part, so the same gap applies to v14. Fixing it changes the decision rules and could change the verdict, so it has to be done before the freeze.

findings.title: Rules 4 and 7 cannot fail; rule 5's training side is fixed in advance
findings.evidence: Rule 4 (lines 881-882) is computed only on the eight earlier sets (mdtest, mdfresh, mdwords, mdblind, mdllm, mdplan, mdrep, mdtick). Development already gives v13 - v11 >= 0 and v14 - v12 >= 0 on every one of them, and answers are deterministic (v14's forms are cached, plan9/forms/form_<set>.jsonl). Rule 7 (lines 887-888) uses mdtrain only: v13 = v14 = 1.000 against v4 = 0.927, already known. Rule 5 compares against mdtrainv9, where v13 = v14 = 1.000 is known, so it reduces to 'test set >= 0.85'. The pre-registration says 4 and 7 are known (lines 126 and 130), but they stay in the rules list next to the deciding rules. Rule 3 is also stated to just follow rule 1, and in development v14 matched v13 on every action-item change.
findings.fix: List rules 4 and 7 as sanity checks reproduced at run time, not as test rules. Make it explicit that the confirmatory content is rules 1 and 2 (plus 5 and 6 on the new set).

verdict.reason:
The facts in the finding are right, but the protocol problem it describes does not exist, because the pre-registration already says all of this.

What checks out:
- In dev_v1{1,3,2,4}.json, v13 is at least v11 and v14 is at least v12 on each of the eight earlier sets. The 8-set means are v11 0.960, v13 0.969, v12 0.974, v14 0.982.
- v13 and v14 both score 1.000 on mdtrain and on mdtrainv9.
- Every set has a cached form file in plan9/forms.
- order_test computes rule 4 from the earlier sets, rule 7 from mdtrain against v4, and rule 5 against mdtrainv9 (lines 881-888).

Why it is not a defect: FACTBANK_ORDER_PREREGISTRATION.md already marks each of these.
- Rule 3: "expected to follow rule 1; it is not a separate confirmation".
- Rule 4: "Known from development, so it is a guard rather than a test".
- Rule 5: "The training score is known: 1.000".
- Rule 7: "Known: 1.000 against 0.927".
- What decides: "Rules 1 and 2 decide whether the check works."

The previous test followed the same practice. FACTBANK_TICKET_RESULTS.md reported these rows as "4. ... (guard, known)" and "7. ... (known)", so they were not counted as confirmations.

The suggested fix is therefore already in place. Rules 4 and 7 are kept as checks that the run reproduces development. If the file-based answers or a form-cache miss gave different results at run time, they would fail, and that is what a guard is for. The only part left is where the rules are listed, which is cosmetic. It changes no number, no verdict and nothing about how fair the test is.

findings.title: Stemming quietly makes 'soon', 'lasting' and 'finals' words of order; 'soon' matters for the test's roles
findings.evidence: ORDER_WORDS is built from stem(w), and stem strips 'er'. So 'sooner' becomes 'soon', and the effective set is {after, before, closest, earli, earliest, final, first, last, later, latest, nearest, next, soon, soonest, urgent}. stem('soon') = 'soon' is in the set, as are stem('lasting') = 'last' and stem('finals') = 'final'. The pre-registration lists 'sooner' but not 'soon' ('(stemmed)' only). An action-item question like '... send me the keys as soon as you can' then counts as asking for an order, and the check stays off. The test's writers are an on-call support engineer and a VP on a phone between meetings, who are likely to write 'soon', 'before my next meeting' or 'after the call'. Earlier writers did this too: 'before my call', 'before I book interviews', 'After "{m}"'. This makes rule 1 harder to meet, not easier, so it is not a fairness leak, but the documented list does not match what the code does.
findings.fix: Give the effective stemmed list in the pre-registration (note that 'soon' counts). Or build the set from exact surface forms, without stem(), so the frozen list is what it says.

verdict.reason:
The finding is correct about what the code does. It overstates the gap with the document, and it does not affect the test.

What I checked:
- ORDER_WORDS (plans.py:51) is built with engine.stem. Its effective set is {after, before, closest, earli, earliest, final, first, last, later, latest, nearest, next, soon, soonest, urgent}.
- Planner.asks_order matches stems, because question_words also applies stem().
- I ran it. 'send me the keys as soon as you can', 'what is lasting', 'the finals', 'lasted' and 'lasts' all count as asking for an order.

So bare 'soon' does count, and the pre-registration's list (line 29-30) does not say so. It does end with '(stemmed)', which tells a reader that matching is on stems, but nobody would guess from that that bare 'soon' counts. That makes this a small gap in the wording, not a document that contradicts the code. It is also unavoidable: question words are stemmed, so 'sooner' in a question becomes 'soon'. The set must contain 'soon' to catch 'sooner' at all.

The finding's second fix (exact surface forms without stem()) would be a bug. With the surface-form set, 'which is due earlier?' and 'which is due sooner?' both matched nothing, because the question side becomes 'earli' and 'soon'. Only the first fix, noting in the document that 'soon' counts, is sound.

Why it does not matter for the test:
- Across all 1,099 earlier questions (mdtrain, mdtrainv9, mdtest, mdfresh, mdwords, mdblind, mdllm, mdplan*, mdrep*, mdtick*), no word counted only because of stemming. Every 'soon' is 'soonest', so the development numbers are untouched.
- 'urgent' is already a listed word with the same effect on an on-call writer's wording.
- The extra matches can only switch the check off. That can only lower v13's gain over v11, which makes rule 1 harder and rule 2 safer. It gives v13 no advantage.
- The code is frozen by commit hash, so what is tested is exactly what the code does. A note in the document changes no number or verdict.

findings.title: The motivation's '8 of the 10 action items got part marks ... in v9, v11 and v12 alike' is not right for v9
findings.evidence: From the stored mdtick answers: v11 and v12 got part marks on 8 of 10 action items, all from a '... -> due_date -> earliest' plan. v9 used an earliest plan on 8 too, but 2 of those (action_owner_issues-020 and -035) took the earliest over the owner's Fireflies action items and scored 0.0, and a third (-029) scored 0.0 from another plan. v9's scores: [0.667, 0, 0.667, 0.4, 1, 0, 0, 0.4, 0.4, 0.4], so 6 part marks and 3 zeros.
findings.fix: Say 'v11 and v12 got part marks on 8 of 10; v9 chose the first-due plan on 8 (6 part marks, 2 zeros)'.

verdict.reason: I could not refute it. The claim is wrong for v9. In /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-integratedai/275b943f-979b-5741-9af5-2a07879accea/scratchpad/mdtick/ticket_report.json (held_out.rows) and factbank_v9.jsonl, v9's scores on the 10 action items are 014=0.667, 020=0, 021=0.667, 027=0.4, 028=1.0, 029=0, 035=0, 036=0.4, 040=0.4, 041=0.4. That is 6 part marks, 3 zeros and 1 full mark, and the mean is 0.393, which matches the report's v9 action_items figure. v9 did pick a '-> due_date -> earliest' plan on 8 items. But on 020 and 035 it took that plan through 'action_owner_of [fireflies]', so it returned an action-item title and scored 0, not part marks. On 029 it used a different plan (redwood_attendees_of -> list) and also scored 0. v11 and v12 really did get part marks on 8 of 10 (all '-> assignee_of [ticket] -> due_date -> earliest'), with 020 and 028 at 1.0. The project's own docs/FACTBANK_TICKET_RESULTS.md agrees: its table gives v9=0 on 020, 029 and 035, and says '6 of them return only the first due, in both versions' for the other 7. So the prereg line 18-19 ('8 of the 10 action items there got part marks for this, in v9, v11 and v12 alike') overstates v9 and does not match the earlier results doc. It is only motivation text, though. v9 appears in none of the 7 rules (they compare v13 with v11, v14 with v12, and v4 for rule 7), so fixing it changes no threshold, number, verdict or fairness of the test.
